newsitem.title: USA: U.S. statistical agency questions CPI panel report.
newsitem.headline: U.S. statistical agency questions CPI panel report.

text.p: The agency that issues the monthly Consumer Price Index said Thursday that an independent panel's report released earlier this month that showed bias in the data relied heavily on panel members' judgment and lacked "hard empirical evidence."

A congressionally appointed commission led by Stanford University professor Michael Boskin concluded that the CPI overstates inflation partly because of the way the government measures improvements in the quality of goods and services.
"Hard empirical evidence regarding the magnitude of biases from these sources is extremely limited," the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics said in a statement.

The agency said the commission leaned heavily on "the members' best judgment as to the value of consumers of various marketplace developments" rather than by comparing CPI against any alternative measure.
But BLS Commissioner Katharine Abraham declined to criticise the Boskin group. "I don't question their judgment," she said at a press briefing.
The panel's controversial report maintained that the agency overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points annually.

The BLS said nearly two-thirds of that upward bias as estimated by the commission stemmed from alleged deficiencies in the treatment of changes in the quality of goods and services and the introduction of new goods.
The BLS said it already makes some adjustments for quality changes when it calculates the CPI.
During 1995, more than half of price changes reported for goods and services were "adjusted out" of the CPI, the BLS said.

"This does not mean that the methods used in constructing the CPI capture quality change perfectly, only that the quality adjustment procedures currently in place have a profound impact on reported price change," the BLS said.
In its report, the panel proposed action by Congress and the Clinton administration but also included technical suggestions for the BLS, which issues the monthly index.
The agency plans to make some changes in the way the consumer price index is calculated, but many will take time, Abraham said.
"We're looking to make changes as expeditiously as we can, she said. "But I don't have anything in mind that at this point throwing more money at us would let us do faster.
"Money is not the only restraint here," she added. "It's skilled staff to do the work."
